html: Minerals in urine can clump into crystals that grow into small, hard stones. Tiny ones may pass unnoticed; larger ones can cause intense pain as they travel toward the bladder.

• Waves of sharp pain in the back or side, sometimes spreading toward the groin
  • Blood in the urine, which can make it look pinkish or brownish
  • Feeling queasy or throwing up
  • Needing to urinate often, or a burning feeling when you go

• Drink enough that your urine stays pale
  • Go easy on salt
  • Ask your care team whether diet changes make sense for the kind of stone you had
The pain is more than you can manage at home, especially with a fever, vomiting, or little or no urine.

title: Kidney stones
abstract: How kidney stones form, what passing one feels like and how to prevent another.
